metadata.note: Yes -- Baton Rouge had real passenger rail service, and it was a genuinely busy hub at its peak, reached by at least two entirely separate railroads from two different directions. The dominant one: Memphis-Vicksburg-Baton Rouge-New Orleans, built 1888-1890 as the Louisville, New Orleans and Texas Railway (incorporating the earlier New Orleans, Baton Rouge, and Vicksburg Railroad Company), bought by the Illinois Central in 1892 and merged into its Yazoo & Mississippi Valley Railroad subsidiary. A detailed mile-by-mile 1875-1976 station guide (see sources) let this route be rebuilt through its REAL intermediate stops rather than just endpoints: south from the Mississippi line at Norwood (330.1 on the guide's mileage), the line ran through Wilson, Gurley, McManus, Ethel, Slaughter, Zachary, Baker, North Baton Rouge, Baton Rouge (366.5), University, Arlington, Gardere, St. Gabriel, Geismar, Burnside, Union, Central, Romeville, Convent, Garyville, Reserve, La Place, Montz, Norco, Destrehan, St. Rose, Kenner, to New Orleans (455.9). This is a DIFFERENT, more westerly route than the IC's Chicago-New Orleans main line already on this map (see illinois_central.geojson, via Jackson and McComb MS, not through Vicksburg or Baton Rouge). By 1928 Baton Rouge's IC depot (built 1926) saw 22 trains a day from three separate railroads -- 14 Yazoo & Mississippi Valley (Illinois Central) on this route, 6 Gulf Coast Lines (Missouri Pacific, which reached Baton Rouge via trackage rights over this SAME Illinois Central line, per the mile guide's Line 32), and 2 Texas & New Orleans (Southern Pacific), which used a wholly separate line from Lafayette (see the second feature below). A fourth company, Kansas City Southern, ran its Southern Belle into a separate Baton Rouge station until 1969, reaching the city via the Louisiana Railway's Simmesport-Baton Rouge line after the 1940 opening of the Huey P. Long/O.K. Allen highway-and-rail bridge across the Mississippi -- before 1940, KCS/Louisiana Railway's New Orleans trains (the Flying Crow and Southern Belle) reached New Orleans via a ferry connection at Angola/Filston instead. Passenger service at the main IC depot ended in 1967. HONEST LIMITATION ON GEOMETRY: this remains one of the most thoroughly-vanished corridors traced in this project. Of the ~14 real, precisely mile-marked towns between Vicksburg and New Orleans, only one short stretch -- Zachary to Baker to Baton Rouge, about 20km -- could be matched to a real, currently-tagged rail alignment in OpenStreetMap (confirmed after two independent attempts with both a 3-point and a 14-point waypoint chain, plus a search for abandoned-railway and rail-trail tagging that also came up empty for the missing stretches). Every other segment -- Vicksburg to Norwood, Norwood to Zachary, and the entire Baton Rouge-to-New-Orleans run along River Road -- is a straight line between real, correctly-ordered, correctly-mile-spaced towns, not a track trace. That's a meaningfully better approximation than the file's previous version (6 sparse points with no intermediate stops at all), but it is still not real track geometry.
sources: SL 248 'Louisiana Railroads' passenger station guide (branchline.uk), compiled from the 1858/1875/1884/1893 Official/Dinsmore Guides plus company timetables -- Line 2 (Norwood-New Orleans, IC ex Louisville New Orleans & Texas ex Yazoo & Mississippi Valley) gives the full real mile-by-mile station list used to rebuild this route's waypoints; Line 32 confirms Missouri Pacific/Gulf Coast Lines reached Baton Rouge over this same IC trackage; Line 22 documents the Kansas City Southern's Simmesport-Baton Rouge access via the 1940 Huey P. Long/O.K. Allen bridge, replacing an earlier ferry at Angola/Filston; Line 64 gives the separate Southern Pacific Lafayette-Baton Rouge route (Anse la Butte-Breaux Bridge Jct-Henderson-Atchafalaya River crossing-Grosse Tete-Baton Rouge), noting a passenger ferry replaced the Atchafalaya bridge after c.1930

geometry_sources: OpenStreetMap (via Overpass API), railway=rail: only the Zachary-Baker-Baton Rouge stretch (~20km) matched a real connected alignment. Everything else on both features is a straight-line approximation between real, mile-marker-sourced town waypoints -- no connected active or abandoned rail geometry exists in OSM for the rest of either route.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.
